content.prompt: Part 1 — The writer in trouble
content.answer: John Hallock is a writer who earns his living by writing ghost stories for Jenkin's magazine — though he dislikes the task and finds it hard to invent plots. His publisher, Jenkins, is pressing him for a new story, and John sits at his desk, unable to think of anything. Suddenly a ghost materialises before him — an owl-eyed, unattractive female spirit. She is part of "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau": ghosts like her have been supplying writers with their plots, sitting on their shoulders and whispering ideas.

content.prompt: Part 2 — The ghost on strike
content.answer: The ghost, Helen, tells John that the ghosts are on strike. Too many people have taken to using Ouija boards, summoning spirits for silly questions, and the ghosts are exhausted and resent being treated as entertainers. Until people give up their Ouija boards, the Inspiration Bureau will supply no more plots. Helen asks John to use his influence to stop his friends from using Ouija boards. John is horrified, therefore, when his wife Lavinia comes home and proudly announces that she has bought an Ouija board.

content.prompt: Part 3 — The Ouija board party
content.answer: Lavinia, who loves new fashions and fads, invites her friends to a Ouija board party at their house. John is forced to take part, dreading what the ghost had warned him about. During the séance the board spells out strange words — and to John's horror, the name "Helen" appears, along with words that make him seem a traitor to his wife. Lavinia, already suspicious, now believes her husband is having an affair with a woman named Helen. She decides to leave him.

content.prompt: Part 4 — The misunderstanding cleared
content.answer: As Lavinia packs to leave, Helen appears to her. The ghost explains who she really is — the spirit who had been helping John with his stories — and tells her that the name on the Ouija board was hers, not the name of any earthly rival. Lavinia's misunderstanding is cleared, and she and John are reconciled. Gladolia, the terrified maid, declares the Ouija board a "hoodoo" and refuses to stay. The board is thrown into the fire, and John, delighted at the turn of events, at last has the plot for his new ghost story.

content.prompt: Superstition and the craze for the supernatural
content.answer: The story satirises the fashion for spiritualism and Ouija boards. Lavinia buys a board because it is the latest trend, her friends gather for séances as a party game, and the ghosts themselves go on strike because they are tired of being summoned for trivial questions. The theme mocks blind credulity: people who play with forces they do not understand — and the Ouija board, meant to be harmless fun, nearly destroys John's marriage through a mere misunderstanding.

content.prompt: Trust and misunderstanding in marriage
content.answer: The story turns on a domestic misunderstanding. Lavinia's suspicion that John is involved with a woman named Helen is built entirely on the words spelled out by the Ouija board — a few letters that are, in truth, the name of a ghost. Because she trusts the board more than her husband, the misunderstanding grows until she packs to leave. The theme teaches the value of trust and communication: had Lavinia asked John directly, the whole storm could have been avoided. Superstition, the story suggests, feeds on mistrust.

content.prompt: The writer's struggle for inspiration
content.answer: John Hallock is a reluctant writer whose inspiration literally comes from ghosts — the members of the "Writer's Inspiration Bureau" who whisper plots into writers' ears. When the ghosts go on strike, John is helpless before his blank page. The theme satirises the writing life: inspiration is mysterious, unreliable, and often felt to come from outside oneself. The story's joke is that John's supernatural helpers are as real to him as his publisher's demands — and that his best story arrives precisely when he stops trying to force it.

content.prompt: John Hallock
content.answer: John Hallock is the narrator, a writer of ghost stories for Jenkin's magazine, though he has little love for the genre and struggles for plots. He is a mild, hen-pecked husband, afraid of his fashionable wife, and dependent for his inspiration on the ghost Helen, who supplies him with plots. He is honest and good-natured — caught between his publisher's demands, his wife's suspicions and the demands of the striking ghosts. His great moment comes when he simply tells Lavinia the truth, and the misunderstanding dissolves.

content.prompt: Lavinia
content.answer: Lavinia is John's wife — pretty, fashionable and given to the latest fads, with an alarming tendency to spend money on new trends. It is she who buys the Ouija board and organises the séance party, and it is her ready suspicion, fed by the board's messages, that nearly breaks the marriage. Yet she is not unkind: her jealousy springs from love, and once Helen explains the truth, she is reconciled at once, and the board goes into the fire. She represents the human weakness for superstition and the strength of a loving heart that can forgive.

content.prompt: Helen, the ghost
content.answer: Helen is an owl-eyed, unattractive ghost, a member of "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau" who supplies plots to writers. She appears to John when he is stuck, materialising in parts — a hand, then a face — like a moving-picture cartoon. She is sharp-tongued and fed up: the ghosts have gone on strike because people abuse Ouija boards. Yet she is friendly to John and finally saves his marriage by revealing herself to Lavinia. She is a comic figure — a ghost who is more like a harassed office worker than a spirit of terror.

content.prompt: Gladolia
content.answer: Gladolia is the Hallocks' maid, a minor but memorable figure. She is terrified of the Ouija board and its works, declaring it a "hoodoo" and refusing to stay in the house while it is used. Her simple, fearful faith serves as comic contrast to the fashionable credulity of Lavinia and her friends — and as the story's sly comment: the least educated person in the tale is the one who most sensibly refuses to play with the supernatural.

content.prompt: Trust your loved ones before hearsay
content.answer: The story teaches the value of trust in relationships. Lavinia believes the letters on a Ouija board over the word of her own husband, and her misplaced suspicion nearly ends the marriage. The lesson: doubt based on superstition or gossip is destructive; love is built on faith in one another. Ask, speak and listen — the truth, as the story shows, is usually far simpler and more innocent than suspicion imagines.

content.prompt: Do not dabble in what you do not understand
content.answer: The story cautions against playing with forces one does not control. The Ouija board is taken up as a party amusement, yet it disrupts a household, terrifies the maid, and nearly ruins a marriage — all on the strength of letters that mean nothing. The value lesson: superstition and credulity make us fools; reason, patience and honest conversation solve what magic cannot. The ghosts, after all, were on strike against being summoned by the credulous.

content.prompt: Describe John Hallock's encounter with the ghost Helen.
content.answer: John was stuck for a plot, as usual, when the ghost appeared in his study. She took shape slowly and comically — a hand materialising first, then other parts, like the frames of a moving-picture cartoon — until a whole woman stood before him: owl-eyed and far from beautiful, the last thing one would expect of a spirit. She announced that she was part of "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau", the organisation through which ghosts supplied writers with their plots by sitting on their shoulders and whispering ideas. Then she made her astonishing complaint: the ghosts were on strike. Modern people had taken up Ouija boards in droves, summoning spirits to answer silly questions, and the ghosts were sick of being treated as entertainers. Until the world gave up its Ouija boards, she warned, no more inspiration would flow. She asked John to discourage his friends from using the boards — a request that filled him with dread, for at that very moment his wife Lavinia was arriving home with a brand-new Ouija board she had bought.

content.prompt: How did the Ouija board party nearly wreck John's marriage?
content.answer: Lavinia, delighted with her fashionable new possession, invited her friends for a Ouija board séance. John, remembering the ghost's warning, was forced to join in, hoping nothing would go wrong. But as the friends sat round the board, it began to spell out words — and to John's horror, they were about him: the name "Helen" appeared, together with messages that branded him a traitor. To Lavinia, the meaning was plain: her husband was involved with a woman named Helen. In an instant the harmless party game turned into a domestic crisis. Lavinia, convinced of his guilt, packed her things and prepared to leave him. John, who could hardly explain that Helen was a ghost who supplied him with plots, stood helpless as the séance's idle letters did what no enemy could have done — they set his own wife against him, all on the strength of superstition.

content.prompt: Describe the ending of the story. How is the misunderstanding resolved?
content.answer: As Lavinia stood ready to leave, the ghost Helen appeared before her. In that moment the truth came out: Helen explained that she was the spirit of the "Writer's Inspiration Bureau" who had been helping John with his ghost stories, and that the name spelled out by the Ouija board was hers — a name from the world of spirits, not the name of any woman in John's life. Lavinia's jealousy, built on a few letters of a party game, collapsed before the absurd, wonderful truth. She and John were reconciled; the misunderstanding that superstition had built, honesty destroyed. Gladolia, the terrified maid, would have nothing more to do with the house's "hoodoo" and left her service. The Ouija board was thrown into the fire, and John — delighted to have his wife back, his ghost's strike and his troubles all resolved at once — realised that he had at last found the perfect plot for the ghost story Jenkins had been demanding. The story ends in laughter: the supernatural, treated seriously, had nearly ruined him; treated as the joke it is, it had saved his marriage and his career.

content.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about superstition and trust?
content.answer: The story teaches two related lessons. First, superstition is dangerous because it substitutes noise for sense: the Ouija board spells random letters, yet grown women build a domestic catastrophe on them, and a marriage nearly ends because of a ghost's name. The credulous pay for their credulity, while the sensible maid Gladolia — who simply calls the thing a "hoodoo" and keeps away — suffers nothing. Second, the story teaches the value of trust in marriage: Lavinia trusted a board more than her husband, and her suspicion did the work of any enemy. The remedy, as the ending shows, is honesty — the moment John tells the truth and Helen shows herself, every misunderstanding evaporates. The values the story presses on us are these: reason over superstition, trust over suspicion, and plain speech over the whispers of boards and mediums. Play with the supernatural, it warns, and you may find your own plot turned against you.

content.prompt: Why can "A Shady Plot" be called a humorous ghost story?
content.answer: Most ghost stories aim to frighten; this one aims to amuse, and it does so by turning every convention of the genre upside down. The ghost is not a horror but a harassed worker: Helen is owl-eyed, unattractive, sharp-tongued, and her great news is that the spirits have formed a union and gone on strike against overwork. The hero is not a brave investigator but a hen-pecked writer terrified of his wife. The great mystery is not a curse but a misread Ouija board, and the climax is not a haunting but a marital tiff. Even the ghost's appearance is comic — she materialises bit by bit, "like watching a moving-picture cartoon". And the resolution is pure farce: the ghost saves the marriage, the maid resigns over the "hoodoo", the board is burned, and the writer gets his plot. The humour lies in the contrast between the grand supernatural machinery — ghosts, séances, inspiration from beyond — and the homely domestic muddle it produces. Elsie Brown proves that the supernatural, treated lightly, is one of the best comic materials in literature.
